newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila's Napocor sets privatisation plans.
newsitem.headline: Manila's Napocor sets privatisation plans.

text.p: After decades in government hands, National Power Co (Napocor) is gearing up for a mammoth privatisation that may include the sale of 30 percent of its generation and transmission companies to partners.
Opening up the country's dominant electric generator and transmission firm to outside investors comes amid increased competition and heavy capital needs.

"It might be too premature to say but we plan to offer up to 30 percent of the genco (generating companies) including the transco (transmission company) to strategic partners," said Napocor president Guido Delgado on Wednesday.
He told Reuters in an interview that the search for a partner would have to be approved by the Department of Finance and the Cabinet-level Committee on Privatisation.
In January, the state-run power firm said it planned to set up seven power-generating companies and sell them to the private sector as part of its privatisation.
Details on the stock sale have also not been finalised, as the privatisation exercise itself depends on passage by Congress of an electricity sector restructuring bill.
The bill, which sets down guidelines for privatising the firm, is expected to be passed within the year.
The balance of the shares will be offered to the public, with about 10 percent to employees.
Delgado could not say how much the privatisation exercise would raise, noting that studies on the company's valuations were still being done.
Under the privatisation plan, existing power plants would be grouped under each generation company based on financial viability, geography and perceived investor preferences among other criteria.
But prior to privatisation, Delgado said electricity rates would have to be restructured, making them more competitive with independent power producers (IPPs).
The IPPs entered the electricity sector during the power crisis in 1993 by propping up Napocor's reserves and easing power outages which had lasted as long as 10 hours daily.
At the end of 1996, Napocor's total assets stood at 458.195 billion pesos ($17.42 billion), the company's latest balance sheet showed.

"The whole package of privatisation and restructuring from our computation will mean savings of $6 billion in 10 years. This is the amount we would have to pay if we are not going to privatise," Fernando Roxas, head of the Napocor's privatisation and restructuring external office said in a separate interview.
Energy Minister Francisco Viray has said Napocor would have to privatise as its estimated $1.4 billion per year power infrastructure investment could not be provided for by the national government.
